title: Sliding Window Maximum
description: Brute force to optimized: rescanning every window versus a monotonic decreasing deque.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given an array nums and a window size k, a window of size k slides from the very left of the array to the very right, one position at a time. Return the maximum value inside the window at every position it stops at.

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Given an array nums and a window size k, a window of size k slides from the very left of the array to the very right, one position at a time. Return the maximum value inside the window at every position it stops at.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Spotlight Sweeping Across a Stage
blocks.text: Like a spotlight of fixed width sweeping across a stage full of performers of different heights, and at every position the spotlight stops at, announcing the tallest performer currently standing inside its beam.

blocks.caption: Report the maximum value inside a fixed size window as it slides across the array

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: nums = [1], k = 1
Edge case: k equals the array length
When the window is exactly as wide as the whole array, there is only one window position, and its maximum is simply the largest value in the entire array.
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask why a single running maximum, the trick that worked so well before, is not enough on its own here.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock tracked one running value that only ever needed to grow, but here the window has a leading edge that can slide past the position holding the current maximum, and a plain running value has no way to "forget" a value that has expired.

Observation 2: Maximum Product Subarray already showed that some problems need more than one tracked value at once, tracking a running minimum alongside a running maximum, since either could matter later.

Observation 3: Here, the key realization is different: once a larger value enters the window, every smaller value still sitting ahead of it in the window can never again be the maximum for any future window, since the new, larger value will always outlast it in every window that still contains both.

Observation 4: Maintaining a deque of indices whose values are kept strictly decreasing from front to back, discarding smaller trailing values the moment a larger one arrives, and dropping the front once its index slides out of the window, keeps the front always equal to the current window's true maximum, confirmed by tracing nums equal to [1, 3, -1, -3, 5] with k equal to 3 through to the correct maxima, 3, 3, 5.

Recognizing that an expired smaller value can be discarded the instant a larger value arrives, not just when it eventually slides out of the window, is what turns rescanning every window into a single pass with a monotonic deque.
6. Brute Force Solution
For every window position, scan all k elements inside that window directly to find the maximum.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every starting position of the window, look at all k elements it currently covers.
Find the maximum among those k elements directly.
Record that maximum before sliding the window one position to the right.

codes.python:
def max_sliding_window(nums, k):
    n = len(nums)
    result = []
    for i in range(n - k + 1):                              # every possible window start
        window_max = max(nums[i:i + k])                        # scan all k elements in this window
        result.append(window_max)
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7]
    k = 3
    print(max_sliding_window(nums, k))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every window position independently scans its own k elements, so no information about the maximum is carried over from the previous window position.
The loop runs for every valid starting position, from 0 up to n minus k inclusive, producing exactly one output value per window.
This directly matches the problem statement, but discards nearly all of the useful information the previous window already computed.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every window is scanned directly for its true maximum, so the result is correct.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times k), rescanning k elements at every one of the roughly n window positions.
Space: O(1) extra, not counting the output.

Limitation: consecutive windows overlap in all but two elements, yet the maximum is recomputed completely from scratch every single time, throwing away almost all of the useful information from the previous window.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it treats every window as brand new, ignoring that consecutive windows share all but two of their k elements.

Why a single running maximum is not enough here: the window's leading edge can slide past the position holding the current maximum, and a plain running value cannot "forget" that it has expired.

What actually can be discarded safely: once a larger value enters from the right, every smaller value still sitting ahead of it can never again be the maximum for any future window, since the new value will always outlast it while both remain in view.

The core idea: maintain a deque of indices with strictly decreasing values from front to back, discarding smaller trailing values immediately and dropping an expired front index, so the front is always the current window's maximum.

Keep a deque (double ended queue) of indices, maintained so that the values it points to are always in decreasing order from front to back. Before adding a new index, remove indices from the back whose values are smaller than the new value, since those values can never again be the maximum while this new, larger value remains in the window. Also remove the index at the front if it has slid out of the current window. The front of the deque is then always the index of the current window's maximum.
9. Optimized Solution
Maintain a monotonic decreasing deque of indices as the window slides.
Dry run for nums = [1, 3, -1, -3, 5], k = 3

blocks.caption: Optimized: a monotonic decreasing deque keeps the current maximum always at the front

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because the deque only ever keeps indices whose values could still possibly become a future window's maximum, in strictly decreasing order, so the front index always points to the largest value that has neither been beaten by a later, larger value nor slid outside the current window.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["A new value is larger than values at the back of the deque","Those smaller trailing indices are popped before the new index is added","The deque never holds a value that can no longer possibly be a future maximum"],["The index at the front has fallen outside the current window","It is popped from the front before reading the maximum","The reported maximum always belongs to a value still inside the current window"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each index is pushed and popped from the deque at most once overall.
Space: O(k), the deque never holds more indices than the window size.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

The monotonic deque is the standard technique whenever a window needs to answer "what is the current max (or min)" as it slides, since it discards values that can never possibly matter again the moment a larger value arrives.
Common Mistakes

items: Popping from the back based on index instead of value, which is backwards. It is the value comparison that determines whether an old index can be discarded.
Forgetting to check whether the front index has slid out of the window before reading it as the current maximum.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["k equal to 1","Every element is its own window and the answer is simply the array itself."],["k equal to the array length","There is only a single window covering everything."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Emphasize why the deque stores indices rather than values directly: the index is what is needed to detect when an old maximum has slid out of the current window.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid rescanning every window", think: a monotonic decreasing deque of indices, discarding values that can never be the max again.
If the interviewer says "why store indices instead of values", think: an index is needed to detect when the current maximum has slid outside the window.
If the interviewer says "what if you needed the minimum instead", think: the exact same deque idea, but kept strictly increasing from front to back instead of decreasing.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why can a smaller value be safely discarded the moment a larger value enters the window, even before it would naturally slide out?
How would this approach change if the window needed to track the minimum instead of the maximum?
Why does each index get pushed and popped from the deque at most once, giving an overall O(n) time complexity?
How would you adapt this to report both the maximum and minimum for every window simultaneously?
How would the approach change if the window size itself could vary from one position to the next?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock, whose single running value is the simpler ancestor of tracking a value that can expire here.
Maximum Product Subarray, whose paired running max and min already showed that some sliding problems need more than one tracked value at once.
Any "maximum or minimum over every window of fixed size" problem, where a monotonic deque is the standard technique to avoid rescanning each window from scratch.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n times k) time, O(1) extra space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(k) space, using a monotonic deque.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a monotonic decreasing deque of indices, keeping the current window's maximum always at the front.

Core Idea: once a larger value enters the window, every smaller value still ahead of it can be discarded immediately, since it can never again be a future window's maximum, letting a single pass replace rescanning every window.
Time: O(n times k) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(k) for the optimized approach's deque.
Most Important Observation: a value can be discarded the moment it is proven irrelevant, not only once it physically slides out of the window.
Interview Difficulty: the brute force is trivial; correctly maintaining the monotonic deque invariant, and explaining why it is correct, is what shows real depth.
One line memory trick: keep the deque strictly decreasing, drop smaller values on arrival, drop expired values on exit.
